summary.value: Applies Early Exit Neural Networks to the actor, where the exit probabilities are trained to match the solution of a linear program solved per state. The linear program maximizes $Q(s,a)$ over the probabilistic exits, subject to a hard constraint on the expected cost, where the cost of each exit is proportional to the FLOPs required to reach that exit.

strengths.value:
The algorithm is somewhat simple, and is novel to my knowledge

I do not know this area, but the baselines seem reasonable

The budget hyperparameter is better than some alternative approaches, in that this hyperparameter guarantees any requested budget constraint is met, rather than being, e.g., an uninterpretable soft penalty

weaknesses.value:
3 seeds total is not enough seeds, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.01315 for example suggests at least 15, preferably more

Narrow hyperparameter search range, with no indication of why those bounds were chosen

Training time can increase (because all exits are trained), as the paper notes

No wall clock results (the paper notes that the dynamic branching is not easily parallelized on GPUs, though maybe CPU inference would more easily show a speed-up?)

The algorithm introduces a `gate_loss_scale` hyperparameter and a `gate_loss_freq` hyperparameter. The paper claims "Despite introducing new hyperparameters, BEXA required no extra tuning budget relative to its baselines", but I am not sure that's fair because the gate_loss_scale range is 1e-3 to 1e-1. That range had to be chosen, and it is not clear to me that it should be the same for other tasks (i.e., beyond the continuous control MuJoCo tasks). Similarly, there is no discussion of the `gate_loss_freq`.

comment.value:
Dear Reviewer,

Thank you for your review. For the rebuttal we will try to improve our experimental results, by running more seeds and adding a sensitivity analysis of the gate loss scale, which we agree to be important to highlight the applicability of the approach. Still we appreciate that the reviewer thinks that the method is principled and easy to tune and we hope that the reviewer might consider raising his score, if the concerns are adequately met during the rebuttal.

In the following, we react to the specific suggested weaknesses and questions:

Weaknesses:
1. Lacking trade-off analysis: The main goal of our work is to reduce inference flops, which is why we have focused on this aspect. This also affects the training time of DRL agents, since they use inference for sampling in the environment. In our paper, we explain that, although training time increases because we train all exits, these costs can be amortised. Generating new transitions samples we can already make use of the improved inference time, thus recovering the increased training costs.  However, this was not the main focus of our paper and would go out of scope of our work. Thus, we left it for future work. 
2. Scalability: It does not necessarily make sense to put a large number of exits into a network. Although the Resnet-18 architecture allows for more exits, the general consensus is to keep the number of exits small, as each exit adds overhead. We recommend 3-4 exits, where good placement of the exits can result in a good speedup. However, the design of good early exit networks is still an open research question and is not the subject of our paper.
Still, even with a large number of exits, the additional cost of multiple heads for the critic should be minimal. Features are shared down to the final layer, which would only involve matrix multiplication with more columns. This can be calculated in sublinear time using modern, efficient parallel implementations. Typically, the main core of the calculations takes place in the earlier to middle layers, and the final layers usually have fewer features. This means that, with the right network design, this approach would still scale well, even with significantly more exits and being still sample efficient as each head is trained per update.

Questions:
1. We are currently rerunning our experiments with an appropriate number of seeds and we will provide wall clock times in the revised version in the next few days.
2. We recommend against using too many exits, as they add overhead. From related work on early exits, even deep architectures can work well with a couple of exits. However, even if many exits are used, having many critic heads is computationally tractable, as each head only adds a small amount of overhead, with the majority of the computations happening in previous layers. This approach has been well established in DRL. One of the earliest pieces of work that we know of to use many heads for learning critics is "Deep Exploration via Bootstrapped DQN" by Osband et al., 2016. They used 10 heads in their experiments and even tested 20.

summary.value: This paper addresses the high computational cost of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) by proposing a method to incorporate Early Exit Neural Networks (ENNs) into off-policy actor-critic algorithms. They propose Budgeted EXit Actor (BEXA), an architecture where the actor network possesses multiple early-exit branches. The decision of which exit to use is governed by a novel, budget-aware gating mechanism. This mechanism formulates the exit selection as a linear program (LP) solved during each training update. The LP finds the optimal probability distribution over the exits that maximizes the expected Q-value while adhering to a user-defined computational budget.  The results demonstrate that BEXA can achieve significant actor-inference speedups while maintaining or even slightly improving the sample efficiency and final performance of the baselines.

strengths.value:
The primary originality lies in the formulation of the early-exit gating mechanism for DRL. While ENNs are explored in supervised learning, their application to DRL is novel and non-trivial. The key insight is to frame the exit selection as a constrained optimization problem. Using a linear program (Eq. 2) to directly trade off expected return (Q-values) against a computational budget is a solution to this problem.

For the clarity of the paper, the problem is clearly stated, and the related work is well-contextualized. Section 4 provides a step-by-step derivation of the BEXA method, from the architecture (4.1) to the core budget-aware learning objective (4.2). The inclusion of pseudocode (Algorithm 1) further clarifies the complete training loop.

weaknesses.value:
1) Lacking analysis on the trade-offs between performance and the computation cost

The paper convincingly demonstrates a reduction in actor inference FLOPs. However, the BEXA method introduces two new sources of computational overhead during the training update steps with multi-head critic and LP solvers. Since the paper considers online RL settings, the total computational cost should be taken into account. Moreover, the paper does not provide an analysis of the trade-off between total computational cost and the performance. It is unclear if the total computation (inference FLOPs + training-step FLOPs) is reduced, or if the wall-clock time for training is actually faster.

2) Scalability to deeper networks with more parameters and layers

One of the main interests of this paper is to maintain (or even improve) the performance of the policy given a computational budget, which hypothesizes that putting more computation (more parameters) will lead to performance improvement. However, the experiments are conducted on shallow MLPs (2 layers, K=3 exits). The paper's Future Work section mentions scaling to ResNets or Transformers, where the multi-head critic design seems to scale poorly. A ResNet-18 could have K=8 or more exits; would this require 8 separate critic heads? This linear increase in critic computation appears like a significant scalability bottleneck that might negate the actor's speedup.

questions.value:
1)  The paper mentions the computational budget of policy, but in actual applications, especially for robotic control, the total wall-clock time will matter. Could you provide more details on the results, for example, on the total wall-clock training time for BEXA-SAC vs. SAC?

2) I am also curious about the scalability of the method. The multi-head critic seems to be a scalability bottleneck for deep networks. How do you envision BEXA being applied to a model with, for example, $K=10$ exits? Would this require 10 critic heads, and if so, is that computationally tractable?

Dear Reviewer,

Thank you for your review. For the rebuttal we consider your feedback by adding further qualitative analysis of the network complexity chosen by BRAX on simpler versus more complex environments. We appreciate that the reviewer finds the method interesting and novel. We hope that the reviewer might consider raising his score, if we provide more qualitative analysis and provide a more detailed discussion on pruning in the paper.

In the following, we react to the specific suggested weaknesses and questions:

1. We also tested our method with networks with significantly fewer hidden units. However, these networks are significantly more sensitive to hyperparameters making analysis very hard, which is why we ultimately decided to test our networks with standard hyperparameters.
In our initial experimental phase, we tested our method on simple tasks such as CartPole, which it performed well on. However, these are often not considered complex enough for publication.
2. We are considering adding more complex, vision-based tasks for our future work, but this would require much more time and resources.
3. Although there are similarities, we disagree with the statement that structured pruning is similar to early exits. Although both are methods of neural network compression, they use different approaches to improve performance. 
Pruning involves removing network weights that have minimal influence on the network. This often occurs statically, for example directly after training. Early exits, on the other hand, make dynamic decisions based on current input or features. Additionally, early exits allow entire layers to be skipped and replaced by other layers, whereas structured pruning approaches often prune parts of a layer. So, early exits not only remove computations, but can also dynamically adjust the computational complexity based on the current state.

However, such differences have already been described in broader surveys on model compression which we linked in our related works.

Questions:

1. In our architecture, yes, although by the time we reach the final exit, we will have evaluated all previous ones. Generally, however, there can be an extra layer between the final exit and the final layer, which increases its capacity over the previous exit. This was done because our architecture is shallow.
2. Are you referring to using the early exit architecture for the critic as well? We conducted some preliminary experiments, however, this approach would not provide any benefits as we need to evaluate all $Q_i$ for training and do not wish to exit prematurely. Furthermore, as you guessed, the capacity of earlier exits is much more limited, which increases estimation error. Using different heads was therefore the most robust choice.

We further appreciate that the reviewer thinks that the method is simple and conceptually improves over soft penalties by incorporating an explicit budget constraint.

In the following, we react to the specific suggested weaknesses:

Weaknesses:
1. 3 seeds are not enough, at least 15 are suggested: We are currently rerunning the experiments with appropriate numbers of seeds, and will try to update the results of the paper in the next few days.
2. Narrow hyperparameter range: We performed more hyperparameter runs than were described in the paper with various degrees of hyperparameter ranges (these were chosen much more widely). After testing, we selected the most promising bounds and fixed them for all methods. Then, we run a final hyperparameter search with a fixed budget, which we reported in our paper.
3. Wall clock results:  We will report the results of the wall clock time when our reruns are finished. We did not include them as they depend heavily on hardware and implementation. Previous work in early exit networks also reports FLOPs.
4. gate loss scale: The `gate_loss_scale` balances the loss between the training of individual gates and the objective defined by the underlying DRL method, which however, can be of arbitrary scale and is also problem dependent, so it is not possible to know it in advance. Thus, we chose the widest possible bounds compared to all other hyperparameters, as we had the least information. Nevertheless, we found good hyperparameters even within this wide range without adding more hyperparameter budget to our method compared to our baselines. Thus, concluding that it can be tuned more easily even without much prior information.
The `gate_loss_freq`(uency) was one of our ideas to reduce training time overhead by reducing the frequency with which the gates are trained, so that they are only trained every few iterations rather than at every iteration. We will include a brief discussion of this in our revised version.

summary.value: This paper proposes a novel actor-critic architecture which integrates early exit branches into the actor network. These branches are trained via the underlying DRL method and use a constrained value-based criterion to decide when to exit, allowing the policy to dynamically adjust its computation. Experiments on MuJoCo tasks using SAC and TD3 demonstrate substantial improvements in inference efficiency with minimal or no loss in performance.

strengths.value:
1. This paper successfully addresses the challenges of applying traditional confidence-based early-exit methods to DRL, offering a principled and tunable approach to effectively balance performance and computational speed.

2. The extensive ablation studies, comparing various alternative strategies, provide robust evidence and strong support for the proposed BEXA approach.

weaknesses.value:
1. From the results shown in Figure 3, although BEXA achieves inference acceleration, its final average return, when compared to baseline methods (SAC/TD3) on tasks like Hopper-v4, is only marginal or on par. Furthermore, performance appears to decline on tasks such as HalfCheetah-v4 and Ant-v4 in certain runs.
2. This paper lacks a comparison of the total wall-clock training time during the learning phase. The method introduces significant overhead: jointly optimizing $K$ exit policies and $K$ Critic Heads, and solving a Linear Program (LP) at every update step. It is necessary to demonstrate that the increase in training time is far outweighed by the improvement in inference speed.
3. The hyperparameter $\lambda$ (Gate Loss Scale) in the objective function has a wide search range ($1e-3$ to $1e-1$). This paper lacks a necessary sensitivity analysis for $\lambda$.
4. The experiments are based on a very low number of seeds for the final evaluation (only three random seeds per environment).
